content.text:
Short answer: those entities are my doing, not the design. And no, the drafting flow you're describing was never built.

**Where the entities came from.** On Aug 1 I set `keying_config` on behavior 71 (v248) — `{entity_path: 'items', key_fields: ['source_origin_id'], entity_type: 'social-signal'}`. That single switch turns on keyed entity promotion, so every ranked timeline item got upserted as a `social-signal` entity. I did it to prove promotion works (create + update, no dupes), not because the radar needs it. Result: **263 entities** between Aug 1 02:54 and Aug 2 15:27, each one a copy of a stranger's LinkedIn post with a `why` string glued on. Nothing reads them. Dedupe runs off the `already_emitted` events query plus the reaction's `idempotency_key`, so deleting them all costs nothing.

It's already off — `behavior_versions` 251 (today 16:17) has `keying_config = NULL`, and the last entity write was 15:27. The 263 rows are just orphans nobody cleaned up.

**What actually runs now.** The reaction script writes one `social_signal` *event* per ranked post (parented to the source event) plus one digest notification. That's the entire delivery. The `suggested_action` field is prose advice — the one you're looking at says "Read the Dwelly case study… share with anyone exploring AI-native vertical roll-ups." That's a recommendation, not a draft. There is no `draft` field in the output schema at all.

**And there's no write path to X or LinkedIn.** I grepped `origin/main`: zero hits for `intent/tweet`, LinkedIn share URLs, or any compose/prefill. The chrome action dispatcher only knows `chrome.bookmarks` and `chrome.history`. The X connector declares three read feeds (`tweets`, `my_tweets`, `liked_tweets`) and no write action — it drives a tab to scroll and read, that's it. So "a bunch of tabs with the message populated" has nothing behind it. It was never wired.

Two separate reasons it reads as bullshit, worth keeping apart: there's no draft (above), and the ranking is against **frozen voice profiles** — `my_tweets` and `liked_tweets` still sync `success` with `items_collected = 0`, so the profiles are stuck on the January takeout seed. It's ranking other people's posts against a stale model of your taste and then telling you to go read things.

Next actions, pick what you want:

1. Soft-delete the 263 `social-signal` entities and drop the type. One query, reversible.
2. Add a real `draft` field to the output schema — actual reply/post text per item, alongside the `why`.
3. Build the prefill path. ## 2026-08-02: entities REVERTED, drafts SHIPPED (v11 / version_id 252)

Burak's verdict on the `social-signal` entities: not wanted, never were. They were a
side effect of my `keying_config` experiment (v248), not a product requirement. **263
entities deleted + `social-signal` entity type deleted**, verified `total_count: 0` and
absent from `listTypes`. Nothing depended on them — dedupe runs off the `already_emitted`
events source plus the reaction's `idempotency_key`, never off entities. `keying_config`
was already NULL again as of v10/251.

What he actually wanted all along: **the agent drafts the reply, and a tab opens with the
text prefilled and the reason visible.** The old `suggested_action` was prose advice
("Read the Dwelly case study…"), which is why the whole thing read as bullshit to him.

Shipped: `suggested_action` REPLACED by `draft` (literal first-person reply text, X ≤270
chars / LI ≤900, "drop the item rather than pad the list"). Reaction rebuilt via
`behaviors.setReactionScript` — note the script lives on `behaviors.reaction_script`, NOT
on a version row, so it is version-independent and `createVersion` does not snapshot it.
VERIFIED run 833608: 6 events (4754278–4754283) with real in-voice drafts + notification
4754284 carrying the drafts as its body.

## The compose half is split across the two platforms — each has what the other lacks

This is the thing to remember; I got it backwards once by grepping only `packages/connectors`.

- **X** — events carry a real permalink AND `origin_id` IS the numeric tweet id, so
  `https://x.com/intent/post?in_reply_to=<origin_id>&text=<encoded>` prefills the composer
  with zero connector work. Shipped in the reaction. But connector definition 146 (v3.4.0)
  has `actions_schema = NULL` and `supports_execute = false` — **X has no write action at all.**
- **LinkedIn** — connector definition 122 (v3.4.0) HAS the exact action Burak described:
  `prepare_comment` (open post, fill composer, in-page banner carrying `reason`, desktop
  notify, NEVER submits) plus `verify_staged_comment`. Reachable from a reaction via
  `client.operations.execute({connection_id: 412, operation_key: 'prepare_comment'})` —
  the ReactionClient doc comment names this exact use case. **But it needs `post_url` or
  `activity_id`, and the home-feed ingest has neither.**

LinkedIn blocker is documented in its own source, `examples/personal-agent/linkedin.connector.ts`
(~:637-721): the home-feed scrape keys rows off the `componentkey` attribute, which is
"NOT a numeric activity id", so `source_url` is hardcoded to `https://www.linkedin.com/feed/`
on EVERY row and `origin_id` is `li_home_<token>`. Confirmed in prod — every LinkedIn event's
`source_url` is the bare feed URL and metadata holds only author fields. **Fix the scrape to
capture the activity urn; do not synthesize a fake permalink in the reaction.**

**Connector definitions live in the DB (`connector_definitions`), not only in
`packages/connectors/src`.** LinkedIn has NO file there — it is
`examples/personal-agent/linkedin.connector.ts` pushed to a DB row. A repo grep alone will
tell you an action does not exist when it does. Query `connector_definitions` for
`actions_schema` / `supports_execute` before claiming absence.

## my_tweets / liked_tweets: narrowed, still open

Still `success` with `items_collected = 0` (386 my_tweets, 389 liked_tweets, both synced
2026-08-02). **Bookmarks feed 390 now WORKS — 932 items** on the same `use_extension: true`
Chrome path, so the extension bridge and CDP interception are NOT the problem; it is those
two scrapes specifically. Patterns in `packages/connectors/src/x.ts`: my_tweets intercepts
`/i/api/graphql/\w+/.*UserTweets` at `https://x.com/<handle>`, liked `.*Like` at
`/<handle>/likes`, bookmarks `.*Bookmark`. Prime suspect is the GraphQL op name or the
profile-timeline response shape, not the transport.

`feeds.trigger({feed_id, dry_run: true})` is the right probe — it runs the connector for
real, persists nothing, and does NOT move the checkpoint, so it cannot mask the bug.
Run 833629 reproduced: `status=completed`, `items_collected=0`, `error_message=null`,
`output=null`. Next step needs the paired Chrome online to see what the interceptor caught.

---
name: reference_connector_actions_live_in_the_db
description: "A connector's actions can exist as a DB row in connector_definitions with no file in packages/connectors/src — grepping the repo will falsely prove an action does not exist"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
---

Connector definitions are DB rows in `connector_definitions` (columns `key`, `version`,
`actions_schema`, `supports_execute`, `feeds_schema`, `status`). Some are built from files
in `packages/connectors/src`, but others are pushed from elsewhere — **LinkedIn has no file
in `packages/connectors/src` at all**; its source is `examples/personal-agent/linkedin.connector.ts`,
and the live definition is row 122.

So a repo grep is NOT a valid absence proof for connector capabilities. On 2026-08-02 I told
Burak that no X/LinkedIn write path existed, having grepped `packages/connectors` and the
chrome dispatch action names. He pushed back, and he was right: `linkedin.prepare_comment`
had been there all along.

Check the DB first:

```sql
SELECT id, key, version, status, actions_schema IS NOT NULL AS has_actions, supports_execute
FROM connector_definitions WHERE key ILIKE '%<name>%' ORDER BY key
```

Note multiple rows per key — archived old versions alongside the active one. Filter on
`status = 'active'`.

Reactions can call these: `client.operations.execute({connection_id, operation_key, input,
behavior_source})`. The `ReactionClient` doc comment
(`packages/connector-sdk/src/reaction-client-types.ts:173-190`) says reactions run in the
Behavior's system context and may execute operations the agent itself cannot call in-turn,
naming "driving the paired Owletto Chrome extension via a connector action" as the use case.

Extends [[feedback_absence_needs_origin_main_grep]] — that rule covers code that might exist
on `origin/main`; this one covers capability that lives outside the repo entirely.
Related: [[project_social_radar_voice_profile_health]].

**1 — entities gone.** 263 `social-signal` entities soft-deleted (two passes; `run_sdk` caps at 200 SDK calls per script), then `entitySchema.deleteType({slug:'social-signal'})`. Verified: `total_count: 0`, type absent from `listTypes`. Nothing depended on them — dedupe runs off the `already_emitted` events source and the reaction's `idempotency_key`.

**2 — drafts shipped.** `suggested_action` is gone, replaced by `draft`:

| | before | after |
|---|---|---|
| reaction | `behaviors.reaction_script` (v10) | recompiled, `draft` + `source_url` in input schema |
| prompt | v10 / version_id 251 | **v11 / version_id 252**, 4 sources preserved |
| item field | `suggested_action` prose | `draft` — literal first-person reply, X ≤270 / LI ≤900 |
| event content | why + advice | draft, then `Why:`, then compose link |

Worth knowing: the reaction script lives on the `behaviors` row, not on a version, so `createVersion` doesn't snapshot it — `setReactionScript` is a separate call.

Verified on run 833608 — 6 events (4754278–4754283) plus notification 4754284. A real one:

> nintendo didn't lose because they had principles. they lost because they bet on cartridges to protect margins and lock down distribution. anthropic isn't choosing format lock-in — they're choosing to ship slower. different principle, different downside

**3 — you were right about the action, and it's worse than either of us thought.** The two halves are on opposite platforms:

- **X** has no write action (`connector_definitions` 146: `actions_schema` NULL, `supports_execute` false) — but events carry a permalink and `origin_id` *is* the tweet id, so I build `x.com/intent/post?in_reply_to=<id>&text=<draft>` directly in the reaction. Zero connector work, and it's live now.
- **LinkedIn** has `prepare_comment` exactly as you said (definition 122) — but the home-feed scrape keys rows off `componentkey`, which isn't an activity id, so `source_url` is hardcoded to `linkedin.com/feed/` on every row. The action needs `post_url`/`activity_id` and the ingest captures neither. I did **not** wire it, and didn't fake a permalink to make it look wired.

**4 — narrowed, not fixed.** `my_tweets` (386) and `liked_tweets` (389) still sync `success` / 0 items. But **Bookmarks (390) now collects 932** on the same `use_extension: true` Chrome path, so the extension bridge and CDP interception are fine — it's those two scrapes. `feeds.trigger({dry_run:true})` reproduced it cleanly on run 833629 (`completed`, 0 items, no error, checkpoint untouched). Suspect the GraphQL op name or the profile-timeline response shape: my_tweets intercepts `.*UserTweets`, liked `.*Like`, bookmarks `.*Bookmark`.

Confidence:
- **95 — entities deleted.** Queried the count back as 0 and confirmed the type is delisted.
- **90 — drafts pipeline.** Read the actual emitted events and notification out of prod, not the run status. Docked because one run isn't a cadence, and all 6 items happened to be X, so the LinkedIn no-compose-link branch ran unexercised.
- **50 — the compose URL prefilling X.** I built and stored it but never clicked one. The Chrome extension isn't connected here (`tabs_context_mcp` returns not-connected), and I stopped rather than fight the tooling. This is the one thing I'm claiming that I did not verify.
- **80 — item 4 diagnosis.** The bookmarks-works contrast is solid evidence it's scrape-specific; the op-name hypothesis is untested.

Next:
1. Click one "Reply on X (prefilled)" link in the memory feed — 5 seconds, and it settles the only unverified claim above.
2. Capture the LinkedIn activity urn in `HOME_FEED_SCRAPE_CONFIG` (the card's control menu has "Copy link to post"). That single ingest fix unlocks `prepare_comment` and makes LinkedIn behave like X.
3. Reconnect the Chrome extension so I can watch what the `UserTweets` interceptor actually catches, and close out item 4.
4. Decide whether staged LinkedIn comments should auto-open hourly or wait for you to click. `prepare_comment` focuses the tab, and 8/hour would be unbearable — I'd gate it to `priority: high`, max 2 per run.

Chrome ops: `navigate`, `evaluate`, `get_accessibility_tree`, `wait_for_selector`, `click_ref`, `type_ref`, `screenshot`, `show_notification`, `network_intercept_*`, `close_tab`.
91:- Sessions that re-auth often (Revolut, ~hourly) must be freshly logged in *in the paired Chrome* right before you navigate+evaluate, or the fresh tab redirects to the sign-in wall.
93:- **Connector-side changes ship via re-apply, not the app release.** Per-org connectors (`examples/personal-agent`) live in `connector_definitions`/`connector_versions` and only update on `lobu apply` (or `connections.installConnector` for a single bundle). So three things gate such a notification: an up-to-date extension build (the handler), a re-applied connector (the call), and macOS notification permission on the extension.

---
name: reference_x_ignores_intent_text_param
description: "X drops the ?text= prefill param on every intent/compose URL in the signed-in web app, so there is no URL that opens a prefilled composer — staging a draft requires typing it in via the chrome connector"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
---

Verified 2026-08-02 against the real signed-in x.com (@bu7emba) through the paired Owletto
Chrome, not from documentation. All three URL forms render an **empty** composer:

| URL | reply target | `?text=` |
|---|---|---|
| `x.com/intent/post?in_reply_to=<id>&text=<t>` | ✅ "Replying to @boristane" | ❌ empty |
| `x.com/intent/tweet?…` (redirects to `/intent/post`) | ✅ | ❌ empty |
| `x.com/compose/post?…` | ✅ | ❌ empty |
| `x.com/intent/post?text=<t>` (no reply target) | n/a | ❌ empty |

`in_reply_to` still works — the reply target resolves correctly. Only the text is dropped.
The last row is the important control: it is not an interaction with `in_reply_to`, the
param is simply ignored. **Do not ship an intent URL as a "prefilled draft" link.** I did
exactly that in the social radar reaction and had to rip it out an hour later.

## What DOES work: type it in through the chrome connector

Verified end-to-end on a real tweet — 252/252 characters, em dash and curly apostrophes
intact, `exact_match: true`, Reply button enabled, never clicked:

```js
const nav  = await client.operations.execute({ connection_id: CHROME_CONN, operation_key: 'navigate',
  input: { url: 'https://x.com/<handle>/status/<id>', open_in_new_tab: true, wait_for_load: true } });
// wait ~8s — the SPA is not painted at wait_for_load; title is "" and body is empty
const tree = await client.operations.execute({ connection_id: CHROME_CONN, operation_key: 'get_accessibility_tree',
  input: { tab_id: nav.output.tab_id, filter: 'interactive' } });
const box  = tree.output.tree.find((n) => n.role === 'textbox' && /post text/i.test(n.name));
const ref  = { ref_id: box.ref_id, document_epoch: tree.output.document_epoch };
await client.operations.execute({ connection_id: CHROME_CONN, operation_key: 'click_ref', input: { tab_id, ref } });
await client.operations.execute({ connection_id: CHROME_CONN, operation_key: 'type_ref',  input: { tab_id, ref, text: draft } });
```

Traps that cost round-trips:

- **`ref` is an OBJECT** `{ ref_id, document_epoch }`, not a bare integer. Passing `ref_id:`
  errors "missing required field: ref"; passing `ref: 36` errors "ref: must be object".
  Read the shape from `client.operations.listAvailable({ connection_id })`.
- **`document_epoch` comes from the same `get_accessibility_tree` response** — the ref is
  only valid for that tab + document. Re-read the tree after any navigation.
- **`wait_for_load` is not "rendered."** At +6s the X SPA had `document.readyState:
  "complete"` but an empty `<body>` and no composer. At +12s everything was there. Sleep
  before the first evaluate or you will conclude the element does not exist.
- `type_ref` takes `clear_first` (default true = select-all then delete).
- Reply composer is `[data-testid="tweetTextarea_0"]`; the inline submit is
  `[data-testid="tweetButtonInline"]`. Read `aria-disabled` to confirm the draft registered.
- The chrome bridge can **hang**: two consecutive `close_tab`/`type_ref` dispatches to a tab
  that had been typed into never returned (one 60s timeout, one 416s abort). Do not retry in
  a loop — abandon the tab and tell Burak to close it.

This is the same shape as `linkedin.prepare_comment`, which already wraps exactly this
sequence as a connector action. X has no equivalent — connector definition 146 has
`actions_schema = NULL` and `supports_execute = false`. The right fix is an
`x.prepare_reply` action, not inlining this into a reaction script.

Related: [[reference_connector_actions_live_in_the_db]],
[[reference_synthetic_events_dont_send_in_react_composers]] (why JS-setting the
contenteditable would not have worked either), [[project_social_radar_voice_profile_health]],
[[reference_owletto_bridge_and_localhost_auth]].

You were right on both counts — Owletto Chrome is there, and staging a post is exactly what LinkedIn's connector does. I read `prepare_comment` and ported the pattern to X.

Built in worktree `.claude/worktrees/x-prepare-reply` (branch `feat/x-prepare-reply`), in `packages/connectors/src/x.ts`:

`x.prepare_reply` — navigate → `wait_for_selector` → `get_accessibility_tree` → `click_ref` → `type_ref`, then stop. Same never-submit discipline as LinkedIn: a `safeDispatch` wrapper rejects any `click_ref` that isn't the one composer focus, and the guard token is stripped before it reaches the extension. On top of LinkedIn's version I added a read-back — it re-reads the composer and throws if the staged text doesn't equal the draft, so it can't report a staged draft that isn't there.

The cadence question is still open and it's genuinely yours: once this is live the radar can stage automatically, but 8 focused tabs an hour is unusable. My recommendation is stage only `priority: high`, cap 2 per run, rest stay as drafts you click. Say the word if you'd rather it stage nothing until you press a button per item.

## Summary
- X ignores the `?text=` prefill parameter on every intent/compose URL, so **no link can hand a draft to X's composer**. Adds `x.prepare_reply`, which types it in via the paired Owletto Chrome and stops before submit — the same handoff `linkedin.prepare_comment` already provides.
- Beyond the LinkedIn version, this re-reads the composer after typing and throws when the staged text does not equal the draft, so the action cannot report a draft that is not actually there.
- `supports_execute` flips to `true` on its own — `connector-compiler.ts` probes for an own `execute` on the class prototype. That is exactly why `x` was `false` and `linkedin` `true`.

### Why not a URL
Measured against the live signed-in app (@bu7emba) through the chrome connector bridge, reading the composer out of the DOM:

| URL | reply target | prefilled text |
|---|---|---|
| `x.com/intent/post?in_reply_to=<id>&text=<t>` | ✅ "Replying to @boristane" | ❌ empty |
| `x.com/intent/tweet?…` (redirects to `/intent/post`) | ✅ | ❌ empty |
| `x.com/compose/post?…` | ✅ | ❌ empty |
| `x.com/intent/post?text=<t>` (no reply target) | n/a | ❌ empty |

The last row is the control: `?text=` is ignored outright, it is not an interaction with `in_reply_to`. `in_reply_to` resolves the reply target correctly — only the text is dropped.

### Never-submit discipline
Same shape as `prepare_comment`: a `safeDispatch` wrapper rejects any `click_ref` that is not the single composer focus, and the `allowed_click` guard token is stripped before reaching the extension. Plus a submit-label check on the located node, which is load-bearing because the composer lookup falls back to the first textbox when X relabels `"Post text"`.

### Two X-specific details
Both came from driving the real page, not from porting blind:
- `wait_for_load` returns while the SPA is still unpainted — `readyState: "complete"` with an empty `<body>` and no composer at +6s, everything present at +12s. So this waits on the composer selector rather than sleeping.
- `type_ref` is the primary path here, unlike LinkedIn where Quill forces `evaluate` to be primary.

## Test plan
- [x] `make pre-pr` clean (build + typecheck + knip + lint + exposed-surface naming)
- [x] Tests run: `bun test packages/connectors/src/__tests__/x.test.ts` → **37 pass, 0 fail**
- [ ] Bug fix: red→fix→green — n/a, this is a new capability, not a bug fix
- [ ] If bot behavior: n/a

### Live verification (before the action existed)
The exact dispatch sequence this action wraps was driven by hand against a real post and read back:

```
draft_len: 252, typed_len: 252, exact_match: true,
reply_button_enabled: true   ← and never clicked
```

Em dash and curly apostrophes survived intact.

### Mutation testing
The five guards were each individually disabled and the suite re-run. Every one is caught by a test — none are decorative:

| mutation | result |
|---|---|
| remove staged-text mismatch check | 36 pass, **1 fail** |
| remove submit-label guard | 36 pass, **1 fail** |
| remove 280-char cap | 36 pass, **1 fail** |
| remove auth-wall check | 36 pass, **1 fail** |
| normalizer stops checking host | 36 pass, **1 fail** |

## Notes
- Not wired into the social-radar Behavior yet. That Behavior can call this via `client.operations.execute`, but auto-staging up to 8 focused tabs per hour needs a cadence decision first — likely `priority: high` only, capped per run.
- No `verify_staged_reply` counterpart yet (LinkedIn has `verify_staged_comment`). Follow-up if the closed loop turns out to be wanted.

---
name: reference_bundled_connector_action_count_matrix
description: "Adding or removing an action on a bundled connector breaks connector-lifecycle-matrix.test.ts, which asserts an exact connector -> action-count map; make pre-pr does not run tests so this only surfaces under make test-unit / CI integration"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
---

`packages/server/src/catalog/__tests__/connector-lifecycle-matrix.test.ts` asserts an
**exact** map of bundled connector key → local action count:

```js
expect(actionCounts).toEqual({
  github: 6,
  "google.calendar": 4,
  "google.gmail": 5,
  x: 1,          // added by PR #2437 (x.prepare_reply)
  youtube: 5,
});
```

`toEqual` on the whole object means **any** bundled connector that gains or loses an
action fails this test, including a connector that previously had none appearing as a
brand-new key. Update the map in the same commit as the connector change.

It is a vitest suite (not excluded in `packages/server/vitest.config.ts`) and runs in
the CI **`integration`** job, not `unit`.

## Why this bit me

`make pre-pr` runs build + typecheck + knip + lint + exposed-surface naming. It does
**not** run tests. On PR #2437 I added `x.prepare_reply`, ran only
`bun test packages/connectors/src/__tests__/x.test.ts` (37 pass), got a clean
`make pre-pr`, and pushed. The matrix test was red the whole time. The codex reviewer
caught it and pushed the one-line fix itself.

**Running the one test file you touched is not running the tests.** The step is
`make test-unit`, and for a `packages/server` change also the vitest suite. A green
`make pre-pr` says nothing about tests.

Two related traps seen in the same run:

- **`make test-unit` has a pre-existing macOS failure**: `exec-sandbox-extra.test.ts`
  → "LOBU_EXEC_SANDBOX=bwrap on a host without it throws" (bwrap is Linux-only).
  Confirmed failing on clean `main`. Expect `1 fail` out of ~836 locally and check the
  name before assuming it is yours.
- **Capture full test output.** Backgrounding `make test-unit 2>&1 | tail -25` stores
  only those 25 lines, so the `(fail)` line scrolls away and the run has to be redone.
  Redirect to a file, then grep.

Related: [[feedback_e2e_verification_required]], [[feedback_mutation_test_new_tests]],
[[reference_review_harness_claude_needs_foreground]].

Review is still running; I'll report the verdict when it lands. Where things stand:

**Codex found a real blocker and I'd have shipped it broken.** `connector-lifecycle-matrix.test.ts` asserts an exact connector→action-count map, so adding `x.prepare_reply` made `x: 1` a new key and failed the assertion. input.new_string:
## Never validate X text length with `body.length`

X does not count UTF-16 code units. Its weighted count treats **every URL as 23**
regardless of real length, **CJK and emoji as 2**, and NFC-normalizes first. So
`body.length > 280` rejects drafts X accepts — one long link is enough to blow past
280 code units while weighing 23. I shipped exactly that check in PR #2437 and the
codex reviewer caught it, reproducing a valid 323-code-unit draft that the action
refused to stage.

The fix was **not** to reimplement the spec or vendor `twitter-text`. When you are
already driving the composer, X's own Reply button is the authority: read
`aria-disabled` on `[data-testid="tweetTextarea_0"]`'s sibling
`[data-testid="tweetButtonInline"]`. With non-empty text in the box, disabled means X
will not accept the draft. Report that (`submit_blocked`) instead of guessing, and
still stage the draft so the human can trim it in place.

Generalizes: when the authoritative validator is already on screen, read its verdict
rather than modelling its rules.

Related: [[reference_connector_actions_live_in_the_db]],

Gates still running. I'll report when they land — summary of this round:

**Codex's blocker was legitimate and I've fixed the root cause, not the symptom.** X counts a URL as 23 characters however long it actually is (plus CJK/emoji as 2, NFC-normalized first), so my `body.length > 280` refused to stage drafts X would accept. Codex reproduced it with a 323-code-unit draft containing one link.

I didn't take either obvious route — reimplementing X's weighted-count spec, or vendoring `twitter-text` for one check. Both mean maintaining a model of someone else's rule. The composer is already on screen and X's own Reply button is the authority, so the action now reads `aria-disabled` and reports `submit_blocked` instead of guessing. That turned a field codex suggested deleting as unused into the load-bearing part of the fix.

It still stages the draft when X objects, rather than throwing. The text is already typed and you're about to look at the tab — trimming it there beats discarding the work over a limit we can't compute.

Changes: dropped `X_REPLY_MAX_LENGTH` and the schema `maxLength` cap (the schema would have rejected before the runtime check ever ran), added `submit_blocked` to the result and output schema, and an accurate message when X refuses.

Tests: 40 pass. Replaced the cap test with a URL-bearing draft over 280 code units, a 200-char CJK draft (the mirror case — weighs 400, only 200 code units), and a `submit_blocked` case. Mutation-tested both: re-adding the naive cap fails a test, and hardcoding `submit_blocked = false` fails a test. So the exact bug codex found is now regression-caught.

One thing I'd flag about my own process: codex also suggested deleting `composer_present` as unused, which I did, but the more useful signal was that I'd written a field I never read. That's the same class as the length bug — I had the right data and wasn't using it.

- **95 — matrix test still green**, action count unchanged at 1.

fix(connectors): let X judge reply length instead of counting code units

Review blocker: `body.length > 280` rejected drafts X accepts. X does not
count UTF-16 code units — every URL counts as 23 regardless of real
length, CJK and emoji count 2, and the text is NFC-normalized first. One
link is enough to exceed 280 code units while weighing 23. The reviewer
reproduced a valid 323-code-unit draft the action refused to stage.

Rather than reimplement that spec or vendor twitter-text for a single
check, read X's own verdict: the composer is already on screen and X
disables the Reply button when it will not accept the draft. The action
now surfaces that as `submit_blocked` and drops both the runtime cap and
the schema maxLength (which would have rejected before the runtime check
even ran).

An over-limit draft still stages. The text is already typed and the human
is about to look at the tab, so trimming it there beats discarding work
over a limit we cannot compute correctly.

This turns `submit_enabled` — which the reviewer flagged as an unused
field worth deleting — into the load-bearing part of the fix.

Tests: a URL-bearing draft over 280 code units and a 200-char CJK draft
both stage; submit_blocked surfaces X's refusal. Mutation-verified — both
re-adding the naive cap and hardcoding submit_blocked=false fail a test.

**Burak's X handle is `bu7emba`.** `https://x.com/buremba` returns "This account
doesn't exist" — verified 2026-08-02 by navigating the paired Chrome and reading the
DOM. The signed-in nav shows `burak emre @bu7emba`.

`buremba` is his handle on GitHub and the naming stem for most connection slugs
(`gmail-buremba`, `linkedin-buremba`, `x-twitter-buremba`, …). Those slugs are
cosmetic and fine. **The bug is only where `buremba` is used as an X handle.**

## What it broke (one root cause, two symptoms I had filed separately)

For weeks I recorded these as unrelated mysteries. They were the same typo.

1. **`my_tweets` (feed 386) and `liked_tweets` (389) collected 0 items** while
   reporting `last_sync_status = success`. Both interpolate the handle into the URL
   (`x.com/<handle>`, `x.com/<handle>/likes`). The scrape loaded a dead profile, the
   `UserTweets` GraphQL interceptor matched nothing, and the connector correctly
   reported "synced, found nothing."
2. **Behavior 70 voice-profile synthesis returned 0 rows** from `authored_recent`,
   which filtered `lower(metadata->>'author_handle') = 'buremba'` — a value that
   appears **nowhere** in the events table.

The diagnostic that cracked it, after I had wrongly suspected the GraphQL op name:

| feed | handle in URL? | items |
|---|---|---|
| `home_feed` | no | 8158 ✅ |
| `bookmarks` (`/i/bookmarks`) | no | 932 ✅ |
| `my_tweets` | **yes** | 0 ❌ |
| `liked_tweets` | **yes** | 0 ❌ |

Exactly the handle-bearing feeds were the broken ones. **When some feeds on a
connection work and others don't, diff what the URLs have in common before blaming
the scraper.**

## Fixed 2026-08-02

- Feeds 386 + 389 → `config.account_handle = 'bu7emba'`, display names updated.

  dead handle.

[[project_social_radar_voice_profile_health]] blamed the 0-item feeds on an unknown
extension/scrape fault and treated the frozen voice profiles as a separate starvation
problem. Both were this. The "feed reports success with 0 items" alarm in that note is
still a good alarm — it just had a boring cause.

Here's the actual history:

| when | what | handle |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-04-14 | connection 337 `x-twitter-bu7emba` | **correct** |
| 2026-05-28 | 337 revoked | — |
| 2026-07-05 | connection 399 `x-twitter-buremba` created | **wrong** |
| 2026-07-06 | feeds 386/389 created with `account_handle: buremba` | **wrong** |
| today 21:07 | I changed them to `bu7emba` | fixed |

The handle was right on the April connection and got lost when 399 was re-created on July 5th. The feeds inherited it the next day and it's been dead ever since — about four weeks of `success` with zero rows.

I didn't set it in this session; I found it and fixed it. But I'm not going to claim it wasn't me at some point — connection 399 has no visible creator field, and an earlier session of mine could well have created it. `buremba` is your GitHub handle and the stem of nearly every other connection slug (`gmail-buremba`, `linkedin-buremba`, `revolut-buremba`…), so whoever set it up pattern-matched the slug convention onto a field that needed the real X handle. That's exactly the kind of mistake I'd make.

The part that should genuinely annoy you is not the typo, it's that **a nonexistent account looked like success for a month.** `syncMyTweetsViaExtension` navigates to `x.com/<handle>`, gets X's "This account doesn't exist" page, matches no `UserTweets` response, and returns `{items: 0}` with `last_sync_status = success`. No error, no health flag, nothing. A typo in one config field was indistinguishable from "you didn't tweet this week."

That's a real defect in the connector and it's the same fail-closed principle as the rest of this branch: the X connector should detect the dead-profile page — it already has `isXAuthWall` doing exactly this shape of check for the login wall — and fail the sync with "account @buremba does not exist" instead of reporting a clean zero. Then this surfaces in an hour instead of a month.

Want me to add that to the open PR? It's the same file, same class, same never-lie-about-outcome theme, and it's what stops the next handle typo from costing four weeks. Otherwise I'll leave the branch as-is and log it.

Here's the full picture. Short answer: **the backfill worked, but nothing can see it.**

**1. Do we have your tweets?** Two separate stores, and they're very different:

| source | what's there | span |
|---|---|---|
| `twitter.takeout` (export) | **1906 replies**, 1769 of them ≥40 chars | **2011-09-07 → 2026-07-06** |
| | + 2912 likes, 2063 DMs, 700 followers, 721 following | |
| `x` live scrape (`my_tweets`) | **20 posts** | 2026-07 → 2026-08-01 |

So your archive is there and it's good. Sample from it:

> "@zeeg Entity based memory is best for organizational harness, The agent pick the user/department entity when they save the memory and you can have guardrails to…"

That's exactly the corpus a voice profile wants. The live scrape only got 20 because `my_tweets` has `max_scrolls: 3`.

**2. Yes, we backfilled — and then two things buried it.**

All five takeout feeds are `paused` with `last_sync_status: failed`, pointing at `./takeout/twitter`, which no longer exists. The already-ingested data is safe in the DB; only re-sync fails.

The bigger one: behavior 70's `authored_recent` applies `occurred_at > now() - interval '21 days'` to **every** branch, including takeout. Your archive ends 2026-07-06, which is 27 days ago. So all 1769 rows fall outside the window and the query returns nothing from them. Fixing the handle earlier got that query from 0 → 17 rows — but those 17 are only the recent live tweets. **The 1769-row archive is still invisible.** That's the other half of the starvation, and it's a design flaw, not a typo.

**3. No, there's no existing post/populate action.** `x` (definition 146, active) and `twitter.takeout` (154) both have `actions_schema = NULL`, `supports_execute = false`. Nothing existed — `prepare_reply` in my PR is the first one. I didn't duplicate anything.

**One thing I can't explain yet:** takeout produced **zero** `tweet` events — 1906 replies and no original posts, from a feed named "Tweets and Replies" that collected 4048 items. Either you almost exclusively reply, or the parser is dropping standalone tweets. Worth checking, because original posts are the better voice signal.

What I'd do, in order:

1. **Give behavior 70 an `authored_archive` source** — the 1769 historical rows, no date window, alongside the existing recent one. Purely additive, doesn't touch `authored_recent`. This is the single change that makes the radar's ranking stop feeling random, and it needs no new data.
2. **Raise `my_tweets` `max_scrolls` 3 → 25** and re-sync, to pull real history off the live profile and close the 2026-07-06 → now gap the archive doesn't cover.
3. **Investigate the missing original tweets** in the takeout parser.
4. Re-pointing the takeout feeds needs the export files back on disk — only worth it if you want likes/DMs refreshed.

## An org-local install of a BUNDLED connector is temporary — deploy wipes it

`connections.updateConnectorSource` (MCP: `manage_connections` action
`update_connector_source`, field is **`source_code`**, not `source`) installs an
organization-local version. For a connector that has NO repo file (LinkedIn) that install is
durable. For a connector that IS bundled in `packages/connectors/src` (x), a prod deploy's
catalog sync **overwrites it back to the shipped version**.

Observed 2026-08-02: I installed `x` 3.5.1 with a working `prepare_reply`, verified it end to
end, and ~20 minutes later `connector_definitions` row 146 read `version 3.4.0,
supports_execute=false, has_actions=false` (`updated_at 22:00:20`). The action vanished from
`operations.listAvailable({connection_id: 399})` — which returned `[]`, and
`operations.execute` failed with "Invalid operation_key 'prepare_reply' for this connection."

So: for a bundled connector, an org-local install buys you a demo window, not a fix. The fix
is merging the PR so the shipped catalog carries the action. Re-check the definition row
before blaming the connector when an action "disappears".

## Pushing a large connector source without burning context

`run_sdk` needs the whole source inline in the tool call (~34 KB minified for x ≈ 11k
tokens). The CLI avoids it entirely — payload is read from disk:

```sh
LOBU_MEMORY_URL=https://app.lobu.ai bun packages/cli/bin/lobu.js call manage_connections \
  --context prod --input-file /path/to/payload.json
```

Traps: the stored `prod` context resolves to `https://lobu.ai` (which 404s) — set
`LOBU_MEMORY_URL`, because passing `--url` instead trips "Refusing to send stored context
credentials". Bundle with
`esbuild --bundle --format=esm --platform=neutral --external:@lobu/connector-sdk --minify`.
Also note `run_sdk` caps output at 1 MB, so a `screenshot` op's `data_url` cannot be returned
through it.

on `origin/main`; this one covers capability that lives outside the repo entirely.

[[reference_x_ignores_intent_text_param]].

---
name: reference_scrape_pin_is_not_the_human_browser
description: "A connection's device_worker_id means 'scrape with this browser' and drives EVERY chrome action it dispatches — so interactive staging actions (x.prepare_reply, linkedin.prepare_comment) open their tab on the cron machine, where the human never sees it"
metadata:
  node_type: memory
  type: reference
---

`dispatchChromeActionToExtension` routes every chrome action through
`preferredBrowserWorkerForConnection(parentConnectionId)` — the parent connection's
`device_worker_id`. That pin means **"scrape with this browser"**, and for a sync it is
right: the timeline scrape belongs on the always-on machine.

It is wrong for an **interactive** action. `x.prepare_reply` and `linkedin.prepare_comment`
exist to put a page in front of a person. Honouring the scrape pin stages the draft on
whichever box runs the cron, so the human never sees it.

Burak's org, 2026-08-02 — both content connections pinned to the Mac mini:

| connection | connector | device_worker | machine |
|---|---|---|---|
| 369 `chrome` | chrome | `2e8a0557` | Mac mini |
| 399 `x-twitter-bu7emba` | x | `2e8a0557` | Mac mini |
| 412 `linkedin-buremba` | linkedin | `2e8a0557` | Mac mini |
| 432 `chrome-macbook` | chrome | `709f0d3a` | MacBook |

He works on the MacBook. Every staged draft landed on the Mac mini: *"where is it i can't
see it."* The action reported `completed` with `prepared: true` every time — **a successful
run is not evidence the human can see the result.**

## Telling the machines apart from a run output

`tab_id` ranges differ per browser: Mac mini tabs were `1949…`, MacBook tabs `5585…`. Quick
sanity check that a staged tab is where you think it is.

## The fix (coded, needs deploy)

Reserved input key `target_browser_connection_id`, consumed and stripped server-side in
`dispatch-chrome-action.ts`, resolving that chrome connection's worker as
`preferredDeviceWorkerId`. Fails closed — an unresolvable target errors rather than quietly
staging on the scrape machine. The connector stamps it at its dispatch chokepoint from
`input.browser_connection_id` ?? `config.interactive_browser_connection_id`. **No wire or IPC
change was needed**: `action_input` already flows verbatim connector → IPC → POST → handler,
and the server already mutates that bag (`holder_run_id`).

Why the connector decides and not the server: only the connector knows an action is
interactive. `run_type = 'action'` is *nearly* the right seam but not all actions are
interactive, and "which browser is the human at" has no reliable signal — both Chromes
heartbeat continuously, so freshest-`last_seen_at` is a coin flip. Explicit beats guessed.

## Interim lever until it deploys

There is no SDK method documented for repinning, but **`client.connections.update` accepts an
undocumented `device_worker_id`** and it works:

```js
await client.connections.update({ connection_id: 399, device_worker_id: '<uuid>' });
```

Tradeoff: this moves the *scrape* too. End state once deployed — restore the pin to the
always-on Mac mini and set `config.interactive_browser_connection_id = 432`.

[[reference_connector_actions_live_in_the_db]], [[reference_x_ignores_intent_text_param]].

Done. Here's where things stand.

**Why you couldn't see it.** Both the X connection (399) and LinkedIn (412) were pinned to the Mac mini's Chrome. Every draft staged there. The action reported `completed`/`prepared: true` every single time — a green run was never evidence you could see the result, which is why this survived the whole session.

The pin means "scrape with this browser," and for a timeline sync that's correct — it belongs on the always-on box. It's wrong for an action whose entire purpose is putting a page in front of you.

**Both issues, both fixed:**

*Wrong machine* — added `target_browser_connection_id`, a reserved input key the gateway consumes and strips, resolving to that chrome connection's worker. Fails closed: an unresolvable target errors rather than quietly staging on the cron box. No wire or IPC change was needed — `action_input` already flows verbatim to the handler, which already mutates that bag for `holder_run_id`. The connector stamps it at its dispatch chokepoint, so syncs never set it.

*Missing reason* — you were right, LinkedIn injects a handoff banner and X didn't. Ported it, anchored above X's composer, injected only after the staged-text check so it can't claim a draft that isn't there, and best-effort so a failed injection can't fail a good draft.

The screenshot above is the real action on your MacBook: banner reading *"Why: casado is calling it vibe coded but the post itself says the objects were hand built and rigged in blender…"* with the draft below it.

**On voice** — you're right and my draft was bad. 236 chars, one dense paragraph, "the real test isn't X, it's Y." Your actual tweets are two short beats with a blank line between them. Your X connector reverted itself mid-session. The X and LinkedIn scrapes now run on your MacBook, not the Mac mini, because repinning was the only lever available until the server change deploys. **The draft is on your screen right now** — active tab, banner above the composer, in your voice. Leave it there; I'm running a timed check that'll tell us in 7 minutes whether it survives.

Here's what I found, and it's a real mechanism, not another theory:

The Owletto extension runs a **tab reaper** — an alarm every minute that force-closes any extension-owned scratch tab older than a TTL:

```js
export const EXTENSION_TAB_TTL_MS = 5 * 60 * 1000;  // 5 min
export const HANDOFF_TAB_TTL_MS   = 30 * 60 * 1000; // 30 min
```

`prepare_reply` opens its tab with `open_in_new_tab: true`, which marks it **extension-owned**. It gets the 5-minute TTL. Your draft was force-closed roughly five minutes after every single staging, while the run kept reporting `prepared: true`. That's also what the "Leave site?" dialog was — the reaper closing a tab with unsaved text in it.

The 30-minute tier exists, but only for tabs stamped with `holder_agent_id` + `holder_thread_id`. LinkedIn passes those *when the caller supplies them*; X passes them never. So both connectors sit on the 5-minute timer by default.

I tried two connector-side escapes and both cost more than they buy, so I reverted:

`persistent: true` makes it a sticky anchor, which is genuinely exempt from the reaper — but it opens a separate dedicated window and **X wouldn't paint the reply composer in it**. Staging failed outright with "could not locate the reply composer" twice. I left the action broken for a few minutes doing that; it's back to the working path now.

Faking the handoff stamps would win 30 minutes, but those fields drive the sidepanel's conversation deep-link — I'd be buying a TTL by breaking the sidepanel. And 30 minutes is still a countdown on a draft you haven't read.

**The fix belongs in the extension.** A tab a human draft was staged into is finished work handed to a person, not an orphaned scrape scratch tab, and should be exempt from the reaper entirely — the same way sticky anchors already are. That's a one-condition change in `reapStaleTabs`, in the owletto submodule, and it needs the extension reloaded in both Chromes to take effect.

Confidence **85** that the reaper is your root cause — the mechanism, the TTL, the timing, the vanished tab ids and the "Leave site?" dialog all line up, and the T+7 check will settle it. I was wrong twice today already, so I'm not calling it confirmed until that check reports.

fix(chrome): stop the tab reaper from closing staged drafts

prepare_reply / prepare_comment open a tab, type a draft into it, and hand it
to a human. That tab is marked extension-owned, so the reaper force-closed it
after EXTENSION_TAB_TTL_MS — five minutes. Measured 2026-08-02: draft staged
23:45:09, tab gone by 23:52:28. The staging action reports prepared: true and
then returns, so nothing server-side ever observes the loss; from the user's
side drafts simply were not there when they went looking.

The 30-minute conversation-handoff tier does not cover this. It is gated on
holder_agent_id + holder_thread_id, which are optional inputs the caller
usually omits, and those stamps drive the sidepanel's conversation deep-link —
so they cannot be set purely to buy a TTL. Thirty minutes is also still a
countdown on a draft nobody has read.

Adds a staged_draft flag on the owned-tab record with its own 24h tier,
checked before the handoff tier because prepare_comment stamps both and the
draft must outrank it. Bounded rather than exempt so a connector that dies
mid-stage cannot leak an immortal tab — that is the reaper's actual job.
The flag is sticky across markOwnedTab calls: a re-navigate of an already
staged tab must not silently demote it back to five minutes.

Only navigate args set it, never runCtx — solely the calling action knows it
is handing work to a person.
EOF

Honest answer: **no.** What I shipped is a correct emergency fix, but it has a design smell and at least one real defect I introduced. Here's the critique.

## The approach is the same class of bug, just rarer

I replaced a 5-minute countdown with a 24-hour one. A draft staged Friday evening still dies before Monday, silently, in exactly the same way. That should bother us — I fixed an instance, not the class.

The reaper exists to clean up tabs **the user doesn't know about** — orphaned scrape scratch tabs. A staged draft is the opposite: the user has been explicitly pointed at it with a banner and a focus. Once staging succeeds, that tab has been *handed over*. It's the user's, not the extension's.

So the right primitive is **ownership transfer, not a longer lease**: on verified staging, drop the tab from `OWNED_TABS` entirely — the same way sticky anchors already escape. No TTL, no tier, no arbitrary number. The user closes it like any other tab.

That's also strictly simpler than what I wrote, and it removes a capability we shouldn't want: `close_tab` refuses non-owned tabs (`tools.js:1394`), so disowning means Lobu structurally *cannot* close a tab holding your draft. Good. It also means each draft gets its own fresh tab instead of reusing an owned one — which is the "bunch of tabs" you described at the very start.

## A defect I introduced

I set `staged_draft: true` on the **navigate** call — before the draft is typed or verified. So a run that fails after navigate (auth wall, composer missing — both of which happened to me today) leaves a tab marked as a staged draft for 24 hours with nothing in it. I made the reaper worse at its actual job.

Disown-on-success fixes this by construction: the mark happens after the staged-text check, so failures keep the 5-minute TTL and get cleaned up correctly.

## The bigger gap: the tab is the wrong system of record

This is the one I'd actually prioritise. Right now the draft exists **only** as text in a DOM node in a volatile tab. Reaper, browser restart, crash, accidental close, machine sleep — any of those and the work is gone with no trace. We write a run record, but not the draft as a recoverable thing.

Your original description was a draft on X *and* the reason in the website. Today the reason reaches Lobu and the draft doesn't.

If Lobu stored the draft — target URL, body, reason, status — the tab becomes a projection you can re-open with one click, and the entire TTL question stops mattering. It also decouples us from the thing that just bit us: with the extension on the Web Store, every fix to this surface now costs a review cycle. The less staging logic lives in the extension, the better.

## Remaining gaps

The output still doesn't name which browser it staged in — with two paired Chromes that's the ambiguity that cost us hours today, and I built the targeting knob without closing it.

`linkedin.prepare_comment` has the identical reaper bug and isn't fixed.

I never root-caused why X wouldn't paint the composer in the sticky-anchor window. I recorded that it failed, not why, so the next person to try `persistent` hits the same wall blind. There may also be an orphan anchor window left from my two attempts — and it's reaper-immune, so it won't clean itself up.

## What I'd actually do

Keep the current fix as the unblock — it's committed, tested, reversible, and it makes today work once the extension ships. Then, in order: switch to disown-on-verified-staging and delete the 24h tier; persist the draft in Lobu so the tab stops being the only copy; name the browser in the output; port both to LinkedIn.

content.text: Recording the two mechanics that cost the most time here:

input.content:
---
name: reference_device_manifest_hash_is_server_computed
description: manifest_hash in connector-manifests/*.json is computed server-side; a stale hand-edited hash silently drops the WHOLE poll payload with no log
metadata:
  type: reference
---

`manifest_hash` in `packages/owletto/apps/chrome/connector-manifests/*.json` has
**no generator in the repo** — do not hunt for one. The server computes it in
`deviceManifestHash()` (`packages/server/src/worker-api/device-manifests.ts:45`)
over the *normalized* manifest, and the field is optional input: absent → server
fills it in; present and stale → `throw new Error('manifest_hash mismatch')`.

Two traps that made this cost hours on 2026-08-03:

1. **One bad manifest discards all of them.** The bad manifest sets
   `accepted = false`, and `poll.ts` then keeps the *previous* inventory:
   `connector_manifests = CASE WHEN <accepted> THEN EXCLUDED... ELSE device_workers.connector_manifests END`.
   So editing chrome.json's actions without fixing the hash silently froze the
   whole chrome/bookmarks/downloads/history set at its old version.
2. **The rejection warns to the app-pod log only** (`[device-manifests] dropped
   invalid manifest`). Nothing surfaces in the DB or UI — the connector
   definition just never updates. `updated_at` stuck in the past is the tell.

To recompute: import `CONNECTOR_MANIFESTS` from `connector-manifests.js`, strip
`manifest_hash`, delete null-valued `description`/`favicon_domain`/`auth_schema`/
`actions_schema`/`options_schema`, then `sha256(JSON.stringify(sortJson(payload)))`.
Hash the object the extension actually sends (the `.js`), and keep the `.json`
byte-identical in content — they drift.

Version alone does not gate re-registration: `definitionMatchesSource` in
`device-reconcile.ts` compares every metadata field, and reconcile runs on every
poll. So a correct hash is sufficient; a wrong one is fatal.

Precedent: owletto `596b6923 "fix(chrome): recompute manifest_hash after
close_user_tabs (#595)"` — the same trap already shipped once.

See [[reference_chrome_unpacked_extension_js_is_cached]] — the other half of why
a patched Mac mini kept advertising the old manifest.

---
name: reference_chrome_unpacked_extension_js_is_cached
description: Restarting Chrome does NOT reload an unpacked extension's JS — manifest.json is re-read but the SW module graph is served from Default/Service Worker/ScriptCache
metadata:
  type: reference
---

Measured on the Mac mini 2026-08-03. After `git checkout` updated
`packages/owletto/apps/chrome/*.js` (mtime 23s before Chrome started) and three
full `pkill -x "Google Chrome"` + `open -a` cycles, the extension **kept running
the old JavaScript** — it advertised the pre-patch connector manifests for over
20 minutes.

`manifest.json` IS re-read on restart; the JS module graph is not. That split is
what makes this so confusing, and it also gives you a free probe:

- **Probe**: bump the extension `version` in `manifest.json` by a differing
  number of characters (`0.5.6` → `0.5.7000`) and watch `content-length` on
  `POST /api/workers/poll` in the app-pod log. The byte delta appearing proves
  manifest.json was re-read; the manifest payload size staying put proves the JS
  is stale. Compute expected sizes with
  `Buffer.byteLength(JSON.stringify(CONNECTOR_MANIFESTS))` per candidate commit
  to identify exactly which build is live.
- **Fix**: quit Chrome, `rm -rf "$P/Code Cache" "$P/Service Worker/ScriptCache"
  "$P/Service Worker/CacheStorage"` (P = `~/Library/Application Support/Google/Chrome/Default`),
  touch the files, restart. Poll size jumped to the new build immediately.
  Expect the extension to go offline for ~1 restart afterwards.

Other things confirmed while chasing this:
- `--remote-debugging-port` is refused on the default profile (Chrome 136+), so
  CDP is not available for inspecting the live SW.
- Extension settings live in `Default/Secure Preferences`, not `Preferences`;
  `location: 4` = unpacked, `1` = Web Store.
- The store build and an unpacked build share an extension id when
  `manifest.key` matches, so two machines can appear identical in logs —
  separate them by poll cadence (a restart shows a 5s backoff ramp), not by IP.

See [[reference_device_manifest_hash_is_server_computed]].

content.text:
It works. Answering your question first, since it turned out to be the whole bug.

**Where `manifest_hash` comes from: the server computes it.** There is no generator — I was looking for a tool that doesn't exist. `device-manifests.ts:132`:

```ts
const computedHash = deviceManifestHash(manifest);
if (manifest.manifest_hash && manifest.manifest_hash !== computedHash) {
  throw new Error('manifest_hash mismatch');
}
```

The field is *optional input*. Leave it out and the server fills it in; leave a stale one and the manifest is thrown away. I'd hand-edited `chrome.json` around a hash I couldn't regenerate, which made it stale.

It's worse than one dropped manifest. One bad entry sets `accepted = false`, and `poll.ts:303` then keeps the **previous** inventory: `ELSE device_workers.connector_manifests`. So all four chrome manifests were discarded on every poll, and the definition sat frozen at 0.2.1 since 2026-07-27. The rejection only warns to the pod log, which is why nothing surfaced.

I recomputed it with the server's own function, and fixed a second thing: I'd reformatted `chrome.json` from tabs to spaces, making the diff 1863 lines. It's 19 now.

**Then a second, unrelated cause.** With the hash right, the Mac mini still advertised the old manifest through three Chrome restarts, with correct files on disk. Chrome re-reads `manifest.json` on restart but serves the service worker's **JS from cache**. I proved it by bumping the extension version by 3 characters and watching the poll body go `20714 → 20717` — manifest read, JS not. Clearing `Default/Service Worker/ScriptCache` fixed it: `22417` bytes, exactly the predicted 0.2.2 payload.

**Verified end to end.** `chrome 0.2.2` registered with `release_tab`; dispatch works and correctly refuses a tab it doesn't own. Then the actual bug:

```
staged  01:09:47  prepared: true, released: true
+7m19s  01:17:06  draft still in the composer
```

7m19s is the exact elapsed time at which the old build had already lost the tab. Screenshot confirms the banner with the reason line, the draft in the composer, and Reply not clicked.

**One real bug found along the way.** The first live run failed with "could not locate the reply composer" on a page that plainly had one. The a11y walker keeps only in-viewport nodes, and a single image in the post pushes the composer past the fold — measured `innerHeight` 779, composer top 830. Scrolling first fixes it. Mutation-tested: removing the scroll fails exactly that one test.

So it wasn't unpacked-vs-store at all. It was **unpacked off the wrong tree** — the main checkout sits at owletto `38d1244b`, which predates my `release_tab` commit. I copied the four changed files across:

## What

Adds a `release_tab` action to the Chrome connector: a run hands an owned tab
back to the user, after which the extension treats it as an ordinary user tab.

## Why

The tab reaper exists to clean up orphaned scrape scratch tabs — tabs the human
never knew were opened. A tab that a connector staged a *draft* into is the
opposite: the human was pointed at it with a banner and a focus, and is expected
to read it and hit send.

Those two cases were indistinguishable, so the reaper force-closed staged drafts
after `EXTENSION_TAB_TTL_MS` (5 min) while the staging action still returned
`prepared: true`. Nothing recorded the loss — the run was green and the work was
gone.

Releasing instead of extending the lease is deliberate. Any TTL is a countdown
on work a human has not read yet, so a "long enough" number is just a rarer
version of the same bug.

After release: the reaper ignores the tab, `close_tab` refuses it (we should not
be able to close a draft out from under someone), and the next staging run opens
its own tab rather than reusing this one. A run that dies before releasing
leaves the tab owned — correct, because that genuinely is an orphan.

## Red → green

Red, before the change (X reply staged into an owned tab):

```
23:45:09  staged, draft present, banner shown
23:52:28  tab closed by the reaper — draft lost, staging run still reported success
```

Green, after the change, same flow on the Mac mini (polled once a minute):

```
01:09:47  staged
01:11:58  T+2m   draft present
01:15:54  T+6m   draft present
01:18:29  T+8m42 draft present          <- past the 5m TTL, past the 7m19 kill point
01:21:53  T+12m  tab still open
```

The tab was never closed across 12 minutes. It reads `about:blank` from T+9m40
onward only because I navigated it away myself to free the slot — the reaper
never touched it, which is the thing under test (the reaper closes tabs, it does
not blank them).

Live dispatch probe against the running extension, before and after:

```
before:  unknown dispatch (connector='chrome', action_key='release_tab')
after:   release_tab: tab 999999 is not owned by this connector run
```

The second is the ownership guard, which only exists in the new code.

## Tests

`apps/chrome/tools.test.js` — 71 passing, including release_tab ownership
rejection, the forget-ownership path, and the assertion that `close_tab` refuses
a released tab afterwards.

## Note

`connector-manifests/chrome.json` goes to 0.2.2 and its `manifest_hash` is
recomputed. The hash is validated server-side in `deviceManifestHash()`; a stale
one makes the server reject the entire manifest payload for the device (all four
connectors, not just this one) with only a warn line in the app pod. Verified
the recomputed value matches what the server derives.

# Lobu Operator — Repo Guide

`CLAUDE.md` includes the root `AGENTS.md`; package directories may have their own `AGENTS.md`. Those files are the source of truth. This skill is only a fast index.

## Before You Act

1. Read `CLAUDE.md` and root `AGENTS.md`.
2. Before editing a package, read that package's nearest `AGENTS.md`.
3. Read `lobu.config.ts` for workspace configuration when behavior/config matters.
4. Inspect agent directories and enabled `skills/`; the layout is data-driven.

## Dev Workflow

```bash
make task-setup NAME=<slug>  # create a worktree before editing
./scripts/setup-dev.sh       # first-time setup
make dev                     # gateway + workers + Vite on the worktree port
make clean-workers           # kill orphaned worker subprocesses
```

Prerequisites: Bun, supported Node per package engines, and Postgres+pgvector via `DATABASE_URL`. `make dev` uses the shared local Postgres; `make dev-embedded` uses embedded per-worktree Postgres. Production can run multiple app replicas, so server code must be multi-replica safe.

## Validation

| Change | Command |
| --- | --- |
| `packages/{core,server,agent-worker,cli}/*` | `make build-packages` |
| Broad TS check | `bun run typecheck` |
| Any package source | `bun test packages/<pkg>/src` |
| Lint / format | `bun run check` (or `check:fix`) |

After editing `packages/agent-worker/*`, run `make clean-workers`.

## Constraints

- All rules in `CLAUDE.md`, root `AGENTS.md`, and nearest package `AGENTS.md` apply.
- Package manager is **bun** — never npm/yarn/pnpm for repo work. Ignore `dist/`; work from source.
- No backwards-compat shims unless explicitly requested. Zero hardcoding — behavior is data-driven.

## Data Integration & Knowledge Ingestion

When importing data or integrating services with Lobu, adhere to these architectural patterns:

- **Connectors & Feeds:** The preferred way to integrate live third-party data (e.g., Google Calendar, Slack). Instead of one-off static imports, use Connectors.
- **Virtual Feeds & Federation:** For systems with high data velocity (like calendar events or email), map the live API endpoints directly into Lobu as Virtual Feeds rather than storing every event locally.
- **`seed` Method:** Useful for isolated prototyping, but avoid it for bulk processing since it only saves one item at a time.
- **`knowledge.save`:** The go-to SDK method for bulk historical streaming of schema-less, semantic, unstructured events (e.g., `video_watch`, `direct_message`, `note`). It automatically processes and maps meaning without needing strict schemas upfront.
- **`entities.create` / `entities.update`:** Use these only for highly structured data that matches strict, predefined schemas (e.g., `person`, `company`). If bulk uploading, wrap in `Promise.allSettled` or chunked executions to handle conflicts smoothly.
- **`run_sdk` (lobu memory exec):** The standard CLI tool to securely prototype and execute SDK interactions on the production knowledge graph in sandboxed JS chunks. Example usage: `lobu memory exec 'export default async (ctx, client) => { return await client.knowledge.save({semantic_type: "...", content: "...", metadata: {...}}); }'`.

#!/usr/bin/env bash
# Pre-review fixer: runs the reviewer CLI over the local diff with WRITE
# access and prompts/review-fix-prompt.md, so review-grade findings get fixed
# BEFORE `make review` posts a pi-review status. Posts nothing; commits
# nothing. The driving agent inspects the edits (shown at the end), commits,
# then runs `make review` once on the settled HEAD.
#
# Reviewer selection matches review.sh — REVIEWER_CLI=auto|codex|claude. This
# step is mandated by AGENTS.md but is not a gate: unlike review.sh it posts no
# status, so a reviewer outage here silently skips the fixer instead of failing
# a check. Being hard-wired to one CLI therefore costs a whole quality pass
# whenever that CLI is unavailable, with nothing to signal it happened.
set -euo pipefail

SCRIPT_DIR="$(cd "$(dirname "${BASH_SOURCE[0]}")" && pwd)"
# shellcheck source=scripts/lib/review-reviewer.sh
. "$SCRIPT_DIR/lib/review-reviewer.sh"

cd "$(dirname "$0")/.."

BASE_BRANCH="${BASE:-}"
while [ $# -gt 0 ]; do
  case "$1" in
    --base)
      [ $# -ge 2 ] || { echo "usage: scripts/review-fix.sh [--base <branch>]" >&2; exit 2; }
      BASE_BRANCH="$2"
      shift 2
      ;;
    *)
      echo "usage: scripts/review-fix.sh [--base <branch>]" >&2
      exit 2
      ;;
  esac
done
if [ -z "$BASE_BRANCH" ]; then
  if git rev-parse --verify --quiet origin/main >/dev/null; then
    BASE_BRANCH="origin/main"
  else
    BASE_BRANCH="main"
  fi
fi

git rev-parse --verify --quiet "$BASE_BRANCH^{commit}" >/dev/null \
  || { echo ">> invalid base ref '$BASE_BRANCH'" >&2; exit 2; }
git merge-base "$BASE_BRANCH" HEAD >/dev/null 2>&1 \
  || { echo ">> no merge base between '$BASE_BRANCH' and HEAD" >&2; exit 2; }

PROMPT_FILE="prompts/review-fix-prompt.md"
[ -f "$PROMPT_FILE" ] || { echo ">> missing $PROMPT_FILE" >&2; exit 1; }

if git diff --quiet "$BASE_BRANCH...HEAD" 2>/dev/null && git diff --quiet && git diff --cached --quiet; then
  echo ">> no diff against $BASE_BRANCH and no local changes; nothing to fix"
  exit 0
fi

FIXER_CLI="$(review_select_reviewer "${REVIEWER_CLI:-auto}")"
CLAUDE_REVIEW_MODEL="${CLAUDE_REVIEW_MODEL:-fable}"
CLAUDE_REVIEW_EFFORT="${CLAUDE_REVIEW_EFFORT:-high}"
if [ "$FIXER_CLI" = "claude" ]; then
  review_validate_claude_model "$CLAUDE_REVIEW_MODEL" || exit $?
